analysis.title: Morgan Stanley Asks Who's Afraid Of The Big Blue Wave?
key_insights: Andrew Sheets (MS Global Head of Fixed Income Research) answers a client question on recent historic drawdowns in cyclicals and momentum by arguing a clearing event near a bottom is much more likely than an end-of-cycle signal.

Cycle indicators do not confirm end-of-cycle: global manufacturing PMIs remain strong (US print better than expected on Monday), the US leading economic indicators index is improving, bank loan growth in the US, Europe and Asia is rising, and credit fundamentals are improving.
Friday's US jobs report showed payrolls surging with no serious signs of overheating. MS's Cross-Asset Cycle Model continues to look healthy.
2s10s and 3m10y yield curves remain positively sloped in the US, UK, Germany and Japan, which is not the signal expected if policy were too tight and growth about to roll over.
MS global growth forecasts for the next 6-12 months remain solid, with growth over 2% in the US and over 1% in Europe.
Tuesday's midterms produced a 'Blue Wave', the strongest Democratic outperformance in the nationwide vote since 1974, flipping the House, Senate and several governorships including Texas and Ohio.

Sheets says state-level Democratic gains raise concern that more regulation could slow the AI buildout. This is possible but not MS's base case, and not a new concern: semiconductor stocks were already down 30% from their June peak before Tuesday.
Even in MS's high-constraints bear case for AI (harder permitting and power), global data center capacity still grows at a +17% pa CAGR to 2030.

The S&P 500 forward P/E has de-rated about 19% YTD. MS equity strategists see the adjustment as having run under the surface for some time, and markets can finish adjusting before the uncertainty is resolved.
For fixed income, the midterms may ease two concerns that have weighed on bonds this year: high energy prices and heavy borrowing to finance data centers.
A slower, more prolonged AI buildout could be good for credit because borrowing is spread over more years, reducing what markets must absorb at once.
Voter unease with the Iran conflict, cited by the Vice President as a factor in the results, could lower perceived re-escalation risk. Oil is 17% below its end-October level.
Lower energy prices are most relevant in Europe, where MS rate strategists favour curve steepeners. MS EM strategists say lower oil helps EM on several fronts.

Broader voter discontent with inflation could reinforce expectations that tariffs prove temporary, and larger Democratic majorities could reduce the influence of individual holdouts in Congress, removing one source of volatility.

sector_views.rationale: Regulation risk to the AI buildout is possible but not the base case. Semiconductors were already down 30% from the June peak, and even the high-constraints case has +17% pa data center capacity growth to 2030.
Credit fundamentals are improving, and a slower AI buildout would spread data center borrowing over more years.

tension_points.theme: end of cycle vs clearing event
tension_points.bull_case: The cycle data remain encouraging (strong PMIs, improving leading indicators, rising bank loan growth, positively sloped curves), and the midterm result may ease energy and AI-borrowing concerns for bonds. Recent factor drawdowns mark a clearing event near a bottom.
tension_points.bear_case: Historic drawdowns in cyclicals and momentum are the type of price action usually seen at the end of an economic cycle, and more regulation could slow the AI buildout.

theme_stances.key_argument: Cycle indicators remain healthy, so the factor drawdowns look more like a clearing event than an end-of-cycle signal.
theme_stances.evidence: We think the latter is much more likely.

theme_stances.key_argument: The midterms may ease concerns about high energy prices and heavy data center borrowing for bond markets.
theme_stances.evidence: It is plausible that the midterms ease concerns around both.
